title: Transparent streaming degradation & SDK patterns (PRD - WIP)
body:
Context and motivation:
We keep seeing two recurring issues in hosted streaming calls: 1) callers experience sudden quality drops when we fall back to cheaper/quantized model variants or when a downstream tool call fails; 2) client SDKs currently expose only low-level stream events, which forces product teams to build ad-hoc degradation handling (often incorrectly).

Goals:
- Define a clear, server-driven contract for transparent degradation during streaming responses so clients can surface UX that explains reduced fidelity (rather than silently showing partial/garbled output).
- Provide ergonomic SDK primitives that make it straightforward to handle tool-handshakes, partial structured outputs, and fallthrough behaviors without large bespoke glue code.
- Minimize latency impact: the contract should be implementable without adding a second RTT for the common path.

Non-goals (for this PRD):
- Rewriting transport (we keep using HTTP/2 or WebSockets depending on client).
- Full canonical schema for every possible tool or action (we propose a compact extensible envelope).

Problem breakdown / signal sources:
- Observed client complaints: "AI stopped mid-sentence and returned a short summary" after fallback which looked like hallucination.
- SLIs: percent of streaming responses that change model mid-stream, rate of tool-call failures during active sessions, number of client-side exceptions when parsing streaming frames.
- UX risk: users interpret mid-stream changes as correctness issues rather than degraded-mode behavior.

Proposal (high level):
1) Streaming envelope uses typed frames with explicit "mode" flags. Frames: meta, token, structured (JSON-lite), tool_event, degrade_notice, final. Each frame is a small JSON text chunk (newline-delimited).
2) degrade_notice frame: server emits when switching models, entering quantized path, or gating a tool. It contains human-readable summary + machine-readable code. Clients must render a subtle banner or whisper to users.
3) Structured frames: when the model is producing typed output (e.g., function call, JSON object, table), it emits structured frames with a compact schema and a stability flag ("partial"|"stable"). Stability transitions are explicit.
4) Tool handshake: tool_event frames exchange a minimal handshake: tool-suggest -> tool-accept/tool-decline -> tool-result (or tool-failure with remediation hints). Handshake must support async tool responses and correlate with request IDs.

Why this shape?
- Explicit degrade_notice centralizes UX policy for fallbacks so engineers don't invent their own banners.
- Stability flag prevents clients from treating partial structured output as final.
- Small JSON frames are debuggable and compatible with existing streaming transports.

API surface (SDK ergonomics):
- High-level stream abstraction: Redwood.stream.respond({onToken, onStructured, onDegrade, onToolEvent, onComplete, onError})
  - onDegrade receives {code, message, severity, suggestedAction} and default UI hints (banner vs inline).
  - onStructured invoked when structured frames arrive, with api to subscribe to stability changes: reporter.allowIfStable(cb).
- Client default: if degrade severity > 50 (server-decided), SDK injects a single-line stable placeholder and invokes onDegrade; developer can override.
- Tool hooks: SDK provides a promise-based helper to coordinate tool acceptance: sdk.tool.accept(toolId, {timeoutMs}) which handles retries and cancelation.

Compatibility and fallbacks:
- Backwards compatibility: older clients that don't parse frames should still get plain token frames (we keep token text as fallback). degrade_notice is optional for older client behavior but recommended.
- Server side: when deciding to degrade, we always emit degrade_notice before switching model or gating tools; we continue streaming tokens under the new context.

Performance/latency considerations:
- Frame size must be bounded (recommend < 1KB typical); avoid large structured payloads in the token stream—use chunked structured frames.
- Emitting a degrade_notice is single-frame and does not require a second RTT.
- SDKs should support incremental parsing to avoid GC spikes for large chats.

Server policy examples (non-normative):
- Policy A: If downstream tool fails transiently, emit degrade_notice with code TOOL_TEMP_UNAVAILABLE and continue generating a fallback summary. Severity=medium, suggestedAction="retry-tool".
- Policy B: If CPU pressure triggers quantized fallback, emit degrade_notice with code QUANTIZE_ACTIVE and severity=high. For high severity, we also mark structured frames as partial until model stabilizes.

Developer experience patterns (recommended):
- UX pattern 1: "Transparent whisper" — small inline note under incremental tokens when degrade_notice severity=low.
- UX pattern 2: "Modal hint" — a more visible persistent banner for severity=high. Provide a single CTA: "Retry with high-fidelity model" that calls Redwood API with model_hint=high_fidelity.
- Pattern for tool-handshake: expose a small declarative mapping from toolId to client callback so product teams need not write plumbing.

Rollout plan (staged):
1) Internal SDK + e2e tests (2 sprints): implement frame parser and dev console to visualize frames.
2) Beta SDK release with feature flag (4 sprints): opt-in hosted customers can enable degrade frames.
3) Gradual opt-out removal (6 months): encourage adoption then enable by default with opt-out toggle.

Telemetry and observability:
- Track events: degrade_notice emitted, degrade_acknowledged_by_client, tool_handshake_time, structured_stability_time.
- Add dashboard tile for percent of streams with degrade_notice and per-customer severity distribution.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Do we allow arbitrary machine-readable metadata in degrade_notice (risk: clients will overfit to custom codes)? Proposal: allow extension codes but reserve a set of core codes and require mapping document.
- How aggressive should server be about marking structured frames "partial" during quantized fallbacks? Too conservative -> bad UX; too permissive -> incorrect data used by clients.
- Should the SDK automatically surface a "retry with high_fidelity" button or leave it to product teams? Proposal: provide a low-level helper and an optional UI component in our React SDK.

Action items / next steps:
- [Ava] Draft proto frame schema and send to infra for perf evaluation (due 2024-11-15).
- [Rohit] Prototype WebSocket + HTTP/2 streaming parser in the TypeScript SDK (due 2024-12-06).
- [Emily] Wire up telemetry events to the Console and add basic dashboard (due 2025-01-05).
- [All] Schedule cross-team review with serving-runtime and SRE to confirm model-switch latency behavior (week of 2024-11-20).

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a "degrade severity" numerical scale 0-100 so UI teams have a simple threshold.
- For tools, include an optional "remediation_hint_url" that points to docs or customer-specific playbooks.
- Keep structured frames minimal by default; heavy payloads should be delivered via a stable object store with a short URI frame in the stream.

Appendix (proto sketch):
- Frame types (newline-delimited JSON):
  {"t":"meta","request_id":"r1","model":"redwood-large-v2"}
  {"t":"token","text":"The quick brown"}
  {"t":"degrade","code":"QUANTIZE_ACTIVE","severity":80,"human":"Switched to low-precision model due to capacity. Results may be shorter.","suggestedAction":"retry_high_fidelity"}
  {"t":"structured","shape":"function_call","id":"f1","stability":"partial","content":"{\"name\":\"get_prices\",...}"}
  {"t":"tool_event","id":"tool-A","status":"decline","reason":"rate_limit"}

This is still a WIP; want to keep it intentionally pragmatic and SDK-first. Comments welcome — especially from serving-runtime on how cheap it is to always emit the degrade frame before switching kernels.
